chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from some of his companions, from Uthman ibn Isa, from an elder from the people of al-Madinah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who drinks water without interrupting his breath until he is quenched. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'And is the enjoyment (of water) anything other than that?'

I said: 'But they say that it is the drinking of the heem (thirsty camels).' So he said: 'They are lying! Rather, the drinking of the heem is that upon which the name of God, Mighty and Majestic, is not mentioned.'

key_terms.اسْمُ اللَّهِ: The name of God — invoked via the Bismillah before an act, a fundamental Islamic practice
key_terms.اللَّذَّةُ: Pleasure, enjoyment — the inherent delight of quenching thirst
key_terms.شُرْبُ الْهِيمِ: Drinking like heem — thirsty camels (الهيم) that drink voraciously and desperately; proverbial for excessive, disorderly drinking
key_terms.عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: Mighty and Majestic — an honorific epithet for God

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to drink water in one continuous draught without pausing for breath in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) was asked about drinking water in one continuous draught without pausing for breath until fully quenched. He affirmed this practice with approval, rhetorical emphasis — 'is that not the very essence of enjoyment?' — and then refuted those who condemned this practice by calling it 'drinking like thirsty camels' (shurb al-heem). The Imam clarified that the true meaning of shurb al-heem is drinking without mentioning the name of God (Bismillah), not drinking in one continuous draught. This hadith establishes that drinking water in one long draught is permitted and even natural, while the actual prohibition lies in omitting the basmalah.
